**Verification policy, updated by user instruction on November 23:** run the tests needed for the changed behavior and its callers, with builds of the affected projects. Do not automatically run the full desktop and Store suites after each method. Broaden testing when shared contracts, cross-module changes, failures or unresolved dependency risks justify it; include the Store variant when affected code or compilation paths warrant it. Retain performance measurements for hot-path/structural changes and relevant rendering checks for visible changes. Label focused coverage separately from repository-wide coverage, and do not infer fresh global coverage or full-suite acceptance from a focused run. Historical full-suite evidence below retains its original scope.

**Efficiency policy, November 24:** group related methods into one affected-project build, focused test run and coverage calculation where their contracts overlap. Reuse unchanged source/assembly, test and tool-version evidence; do not repeat documentation discovery or verification without drift, a failure or a new risk. Tests-only batches require no new performance timing when production bytes match. For production changes, establish passing focused tests and useful CRAP results before starting the affected structural/hot-path performance comparison, and retain the original evidence. Park documented blockers and rejected approaches while actionable methods above50 remain. Limit an inconclusive candidate to one targeted diagnostic follow-up; if preservation still cannot be established, retain the finding, restore only that candidate and continue to another high-risk method. Update shared reports once per batch, without duplicating per-method infrastructure.

## Gauge centering defect fixed (November 25, 2026)

The separately authorized appearance fix changes the six full-size readouts and compact readout construction from 10/8 to 9/9 horizontal margins. Total inset and available content width remain 18 DIPs. The original one-DIP offset is removed without changing gauge geometry, sampling, saved settings or the smoke diagnostic tolerance.

`ArcReadoutsStayCenteredInFullAndCompactColumns` covers 48 combinations of full/compact view, 1000/836-DIP width, optional second disk, Dark/Light and Bowl/Needle/SegmentedArc. Before production edits, 24 full-size cases fail the expected center assertions and 24 compact cases pass. Afterward all 48 pass. `GaugeWorkflowPassesCenteringBeforeCancellationAndCapture` replaces the known-failure expectation with positive geometry checks and verifies cancellation before image output, preserving the existing fixture-data and lifecycle assertions.

Both Default and Store pass 93 focused gauge/compact tests each, zero failures/skips. Both repository Verify runs pass application/solution and benchmark builds with zero compiler warnings/errors, plus gauges and compact smoke modes. Full suites were deliberately skipped; focused tests were run separately. Each variant produces 51 gauge and 106 compact PNGs. All Default captures were reviewed in seven contact sheets and a full-resolution bowl image; 146 same-name Store captures are byte-identical, and the remaining content/native/live/Settings differences were reviewed separately. Store uses the existing documented WPF-content fallback for five native backdrops;its native caption is not verified. This supersedes the historical bowl-centering appearance blocker, not every open appearance/performance scope.

Evidence is retained in `artifacts/gauge-centering-fix/`: baseline/final/Store TRX,build logs and binlogs,Default/Store Verify logs,render comparison and visual-review sheets. This cosmetic change adds no algorithm,hot-path work or content width;no timing benchmark or performance improvement is claimed. The CRAP inventory remains the last measured mixed snapshot, not a new coverage run:198 original methods scoring at most 30, 142 above 30 including 32 above 50. Other goal blockers remain;historical batch claims below describe their original snapshots. See [gauge centering design](design/GAUGE-CENTERING.md).

### Existing issue retained

RefreshVisiblePresentation calls UpdateResources, which calls UpdateMetricDetails, before UpdateMetricGauges. A valid→missing frame therefore updates details while the active gauge still has its preceding level; the gauge is then hidden. Recovery to zero similarly leaves open details missing for that update. At the exact peak-window expiration, open details can still show the expired high peak until reopened. Full and compact cases reproduce it. `artifacts/crap/gauge-peak/existing-defect.md` records source locations, triggers, observed results and a separate follow-up requiring refresh-order/reentrancy/notification/performance review. Production remains unchanged.

### Likely existing compact trace defect — unchanged

Original-code reproduction uses three one-second CPU readings10%,90%,30%, a600-second window,40DIP height and gridless compact chart. At100DIP width, two bins produce vertices(99.75,20)/(100,28) and visible red pixels. DrawSegment checks singleton input before binning and does not revisit its dot path after averaging. This is a likely existing rendering defect; installed-app frequency, other DPI modes and tile configurations have not been measured.

The current behavior is deliberately characterized and preserved. Separate evidence, unchanged source hash, positive control, scope and a potential follow-up are in `artifacts/crap/cpu-trace-segments/existing-single-bin-trace-defect.md`. A behavior-changing repair is not silently included in a behavior-preserving remediation batch. Passing characterization does not make the missing trace correct product behavior.

### Existing defect discovered — behavior left unchanged

The first expanded original run passed14 and failed `NormalCloseDeletesOptOutHistoryAndSavesOptInHistory(False)` with **InvalidOperationException: cannot Close while a Window is closing**, at **MainWindow.xaml.cs1272**. Its exact original source/TRX/log are preserved under `artifacts/crap/normal-shutdown/original-failing-tests/`. When every await completes synchronously, the async-void handler reaches its final Close before WPF's initial Closing event returns. A deterministic diagnostic/no-pending-work test reproduces and explicitly expects that existing exception. It does not establish successful shutdown or fix the defect.

Successful persistence cases now explicitly identify and test the awaited-work partition; their assertions are retained. The original failed normal case remains evidence of the uncorrected immediate-completion partition. No test is skipped, no finding is suppressed and no production behavior was silently changed. The observation used a hidden isolated normal window and a deterministic diagnostic reproduction; a shown production window with live sampling was not exercised, so real-world frequency and whole-app impact remain unverified. App's existing dispatcher exception handler logs the exception; this batch does not claim to reproduce a live production crash.

See `artifacts/crap/normal-shutdown/existing-defect.md` for the failure stack, scope and separate fix recommendation. A fix must review asynchronous close continuation, disposal, repeated-close and update-commit semantics. Separately, existing preference-save failure skips the following normal-history save; that coupling is recorded without changing it. Normal opt-out deleting history differs from session-end opt-out preserving it.

The two private methods separate endpoint counts from traffic status; they add no new data abstraction, dependency, native operation or managed allocation path. Public/internal APIs, retained windows, logging, exceptions and sampling ownership are unchanged. ### Performance: rejected allocation and guarded fix

The first candidate moved the entire control guard into an unconditionally called private helper. It passed all 110 focused tests and exact menu comparisons, but eight original/current process pairs detected a real **40 B/menu increase on the minimal, unconfigured-control path**: 11,720.4008 → 11,760.4008 B/menu, allocation ratio 95% CI 1.00341274–1.00341288. It was rejected. Its source, DLL, all raw samples and the failed summary remain under `rejected-unconditional-helper/` and `after-unconditional/`; original root `perf-*.json` also remain. No threshold was weakened or sample excluded.

IL metadata confirms that the helper starts with allocation of its captured-callback closure, before its inner guard. The guarded candidate leaves the initial `_canControl` binding check at the caller, so unconfigured menus do not enter the helper. The remaining binding checks and body stay in the helper in their original order. The nullable assertion adds no runtime check or native operation. The guarded candidate is measured again from the original baseline; its results are separate under `guarded-performance/`.

Before candidate comparison, eight same-binary process pairs pass the unchanged latency/allocation gate for minimal, control-only and full menus. The direct benchmark uses actual frozen production DLLs in isolated WPF processes, fixed cultures, balanced process/warm-up order, the same selected allowed CPU, tiering disabled, 500 ms warm-up, adaptive batches, seven alternating batches per workload and GC outside timing. All 16 original/candidate menu/header/icon/help/read/no-action snapshots are checked outside timing before and after measurement. Callback tracing is identical on both sides; no real control is invoked. Allocation is managed UI-thread allocation, and timings include menu preparation with fake read callbacks, not native-control latency.

The guarded comparison passes the unchanged gate across all 16 scenarios and eight process pairs: no statistically detected latency or allocation regression. Every allocation median matches its original counterpart; allocation ratio intervals are 1–1. Minimal menus now allocate 11,720.4481 B/menu on both sides. Latency intervals are wide (for example, unavailable rows span 0.8611–1.5586), so these data do not establish tight latency equivalence. All process samples remain available.

**26 NUnit 4 cases pass against the unchanged original implementation.** They pin literal markup and Unicode, exact removal of ESC/C0/format/bidi controls, row order, header/note placement, empty inputs, lazy cached cells, details remaining unread, caller-owned writer lifetime, original exception identity and parent-command failure handling. ### Performance

Actual original/current assemblies were loaded in separate strongly held contexts, with shared typed prepared fixtures and cached delegates. All 98 raw ANSI/text/state outcomes were compared twice per process, including first-render state changes; outcomes were checked again after each measured workload. Eight representative cases each measure view construction and full string rendering: **16 workloads × eight paired processes × seven alternating batches**. Load/warm/start order reverses in half the processes. Each side warms 500 ms; calibration targets at least 25 ms, then approximately 40 ms measurement batches within fixed operation bounds. Setup, delegates and complete fingerprints remain outside timing. Tiered compilation is disabled for this warmed comparison. No owned build, test, coverage analysis or profiler overlaps the timed run.

No statistically detected latency or allocation regression was found. Every median allocation decreases; common paths save approximately 32 B/call and details approximately 8 B/call. The extraction removes the original unconditional heap capture of marker/settings state: the marker uses a stack capture and the details capture is acquired only on that branch. Raw allocation medians include ordinary harness/library cache activity and therefore are not all integral. Timing estimates do rise in some cases: small-view construction has paired geometric ratio 1.01706 with 95% interval 0.99999–1.03442; active-connections rendering has the widest bound, 1.09684. These data permit a latency regression up to about **9.7%** at that bound and do not prove zero regression. All accepted samples are retained; no performance-driven hint, selective rerun or filtering was used.

## Event log enumeration attempt — rejected on performance

Following the request to prioritize scores above 50, examined `WindowsHistoryEventReader.ReadLog` (82.5). Its native loop has reasonable complexity but needs deterministic deadline, cancellation, error and resource-lifetime coverage. Forty-five cases passed against a source-verified original-body projection before production edits. The same assertions passed against a proposed controlled core, alongside related tests (173 focused cases). Native query flags, 50 ms reads, error capture, lazy opening, shared budget and SafeHandle ownership were preserved by source checks.

Eight workloads, each measured in eight paired processes with seven alternating batches, found an unacceptable latency cost from the proposed interfaces. The 16-event simulated path had geometric mean time ratio 1.39 (95% interval approximately 1.32–1.47); one-event, retry and early-dispose paths also had detected slowdowns. Allocations fell by exactly 80 bytes per enumeration (ordinary 216 → 136 B), but that does not satisfy the performance requirement. All raw measurements and rejected sources remain in `artifacts/crap/event-log-enumeration/`.

**The production change was restored byte-for-byte to its verified baseline.** The projected fixture is retained only under ignored artifacts; no copied control-flow test or unused production boundary remains in the repository tests. The inventory still contains this finding. Actual original/proposed native reads of a fixed future empty range returned identical complete/empty results without writing logs. Those sequential native checks are functional evidence, not a paired native benchmark or grounds for dismissing the controlled regression. Actual unstarted iterator creation measured 184 → 104 B, consistent with the controlled allocation result.

## Measurement and baseline

Baseline: clean checkout `e33267b`. Windows x64, SDK 10.0.404 selected by the repository's 10.0.402/latestPatch pin, `net10.0`, NUnit 4.6.1, Microsoft.NET.Test.Sdk 18.12.0 and NUnit3TestAdapter 5.2.0. Coverage used the already-installed dotnet-coverage 18.6.2 and unchanged `tools/Coverage.settings.xml`. No dependencies were added.

CRAP = `complexity² × (1 − covered executable lines / executable lines)³ + complexity`. Complexity is the coverage provider's machine-produced per-method metric, not a manual source count or Roslyn metric. Absolute values can differ with another provider. The same provider and configuration were used before and after. For example, incident validation scored `132² × (1 − 0.9795918367346939)³ + 132 = 132.1481`; its replacement scores `20² × (1 − 1)³ + 20 = 20`.

The inventory includes compiler-generated state machines and lambdas that implement authored logic, and separate compiled copies of shared source in different assemblies. The totals therefore describe reported compiled methods, not unique source declarations. Generated resource and `obj` sources remain excluded by the existing configuration.

The first sandbox run failed Windows pipe/ACL tests. Both the clean baseline and final verification ran outside that sandbox. The failed sandbox report was not used as the comparison baseline.

## Flow validation and frame batch

This focused batch extracts `ValidFlowReading` from the flow-accumulation loop and `FlowRateState` from frame construction. Flow validation is kept distinct from `SnapshotFlowIdentities`: the latter checks endpoint identity but deliberately does not reject negative counters. Reusing one predicate for both would change which flows are considered current. The new helpers retain short-circuit evaluation and return ordinary values; the flow-rate pair is a value tuple, not a heap-allocated wrapper. There are no public API, model, persistence, I/O, locking or caller changes.

|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|

| `ProcessNetworkSession.Frame` | 36 | 22 | 100% | 100% | Separate flow eligibility/quality from process eligibility and frame projection |

Original complexity was 38 and 36 respectively; final complexity is 24 and 22. Both new helpers have complexity/CRAP 14. All four methods have 100% line and branch coverage in the focused suite. With the 33 added characterization cases, the original implementation already reached 100% line/branch coverage, but its scores remained 38 and 36. Thus tests alone could not clear the threshold. All 79 focused tests pass against both the original and refactored implementations, with their TRX reports parsed.

`ValidFlowReading` carries one `AggressiveInlining` hint because it runs for every flow in the accounting loop. A direct comparison of the split predicate without/with that hint measured 22.83/22.47 µs per mixed-quality snapshot, with identical output and allocation. This small timing difference is not a guarantee; the hint asks the JIT to inline the extracted predicate and retain the intended runtime loop shape. Final verification and benchmarks include the hint.

### Existing behavior requiring a separate decision

A flow whose local or remote endpoint is null throws `NullReferenceException`; an empty endpoint instead marks flow coverage incomplete and skips the reading. The exception occurs after process accumulation but before the snapshot checkpoint. This is a potential existing robustness issue at the portable boundary, captured by `Add_NullFlowEndpointPreservesExistingExceptionAndRecovery` and preserved here. Production reachability through upstream wire validation was not established. Changing it to a clean rejection would be a separate behavior change. The existing checked `OverflowException` for an unrepresentable retention interval is also preserved.

### Existing behavior requiring a separate decision

A representable interval ending before UTC January 8, year 1 can accumulate a bucket and advance its checkpoint, then throw `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` during seven-day pruning. Underflow of the interval start is instead caught before mutation. A forced null `Resources` throws `NullReferenceException` after the CPU reading and checkpoint have been accumulated. Tests preserve both partial-update contracts and subsequent recovery. These are boundary robustness issues; normal system-clock/resource construction reachability was not established, and this batch does not silently change them. Positive intervals below DateTime tick precision also advance the checkpoint and consume the pending restart marker without producing a bucket; that existing behavior is characterized and retained.

### Existing behavior requiring a separate decision

Despite the method's “Never throws” summary, malformed preflight collections and the initial clock callback can throw before the catch block. An invalid NUL-containing path can reach a custom temporary-file factory, then `TryDelete` can throw `ArgumentException` during failure cleanup; that exception is not among the helper's caught types. The initial characterization assumed the path would fail before the factory; the original implementation disproved it. The corrected test pins the actual callback and cleanup behavior, and the failed assumption is retained in `initial-assumption.log`. These are existing contract/robustness issues, documented rather than silently changed here.

### Existing behavior retained

History warming-up readings can supply a baseline, while a warming-up end frame is unavailable. Negative requested intervals behave as cumulative mode at this direct API, although `ConnectionQuery` rejects them at its own boundary. Baseline duplicates keep the first reading even if invalid; end duplicates keep the first valid contribution, but any invalid duplicate marks completeness false. Malformed required collections propagate null-reference exceptions. These characterized behaviors were not silently tightened or corrected; any policy change needs separate review.

## Capture-rule engine batch

`CaptureRules` separates application/service process selection (`ScopedProcesses`) from network-rate accumulation (`NetworkValue`). Scoped CPU conversion to percent of one logical processor now belongs to `ScopedValue`, alongside memory/Mbps conversion, so `Observe` no longer repeats targeted CPU classification. The sum and multiplication order, missing-reading checks and sample-validity gate are preserved. Empty/unavailable selections return a shared empty array; malformed service member lists still throw at the existing count access. No traversal, collection type, I/O, dependency or inlining hint was added. Normalization, public rule models, caller report writing/notifications and `Step` state transitions are unchanged.

### Coverage and existing-behavior limits

MonCore line coverage shifts from 97.71% to 97.69%: `CaptureRuleSetting.IsProcessCpu` is retained as a public compatibility member but no longer called internally, so its one line/four branches are unvisited by this test run (CRAP 20, below threshold). The changed engine stages remain fully covered; this is an identified consequence of removing redundant internal classification, not a suppressed finding. Other unchanged MonCore methods retain their previous covered-line/branch counts. Repository totals are 62.0% line / 58.7% branch; both global targets remain unmet.

Existing behavior is explicit: targeted inputs are evaluated before a gap suppresses firing, machine values before their validity gate, duplicate/backward/sparse moments still count samples, duplicate metric settings share state by metric, and network timestamps are not aligned here. Positive infinity can fire; NaN cannot. Those are preserved observations, not new validation guarantees or silent policy fixes. Normal callers supply ordered samples and one rule per metric; malformed direct inputs continue to expose the documented exceptions. These fixtures do not establish native collection, report filesystem reliability, notifications, macOS execution or whole-app performance equivalence.

Paired timing intervals include 1 (0.913–1.066 / 0.879–1.015 / 0.930–1.024), so no consistent slowdown was detected; equivalence remains unproven and the approximately 1% higher application median warrants that precision limit. An initial short-batch machine slowdown was investigated and not reproduced with longer batches, without production changes. Both raw passes and their summaries are retained, with details in the [performance history](PERFORMANCE-HISTORY.md#capture-rule-engine-refactoring-november-21-2026).

### Clock safety and characterization sequence

The original private path reads `Stopwatch.GetTimestamp()` once; neither sample time, queued arrival time nor the source test harness controls expiry. The smallest seam is an internal timestamp-taking overload in existing Stopwatch units. The original private entry delegates with that same single real-clock read, preserving the public constructor and API, without a provider field, ambient override, DI setup or dependency package. Stopwatch elapsed conversion is unchanged. A new provider/frequency abstraction would add state and change more of this narrow path than passing its already-required final timestamp.

Before production changes, **16 public-flow cases** were added to the existing `MonitorSessionTests` harness: all **63** selected session/portable-identity tests passed against the preserved original DLL. The seam alone then built with zero warnings/errors. Its body following timestamp acquisition is text-identical to the original, with matching normalized-source hashes in `seam-equivalence.json` and frozen `seam.cs`/DLL/PDB. **35 deterministic cache cases** then passed against that timestamp-only implementation before metadata extraction. All **98** selected cases pass against the final implementation with identical seam/final TRX identities. The 35 controlled-clock cases cannot run against the original binary's inaccessible real clock; that limit is explicit, rather than presented as original-binary boundary coverage.

| Reject an unrelated service without taking ownership of the caller handle or changing its permissions | `UnrelatedServiceConfigurationIsRejectedWithoutClosingTheCallerHandleOrChangingItsAcl`: EventLog query/configuration and read-control rights, exact rejection, usable open handle and identical ACL bytes |

Tests bind the existing private imports and query boundaries with typed delegates, using the existing friend assembly. No new P/Invoke declaration, production seam, dependency, public API or native operation was added. Manager handles request only `SC_MANAGER_CONNECT`; service handles request configuration query and/or `READ_CONTROL`. No test starts, stops, creates, deletes or reconfigures a service or changes an ACL. Handles are owned by independent `using` scopes. EventLog assertions depend on the host's normal protected Windows service ACL; the explicit positive case additionally depends on an installed matching WinMon service and query permission. These are native Windows integration cases, not isolated portable unit tests.

**Preserved diagnostic precedence:** an invalid handle or denied first query returns the existing bounded-size error before any Win32 access-denied diagnostic. Null and disposed handles fail through the .NET 10 interop boundary. These observations were pinned, not silently changed. Oversized native responses and failures/races during the second native query have not been injected. The controlled connection acknowledges client publication by signaling the next snapshot request; two sequential frame publications drain previously captured options before applying the new snapshot. A synthetic large positive snapshot frequency keeps physical delivery jitter below the service-staleness boundary; these tests characterize query policy, not physical QPC/staleness policy, which has separate session tests. Subscribing resets owner metadata, so fixture priming occurs after that reset. Warmup cancellation retains its existing derived `TaskCanceledException` contract. The final cleanup check drops the fixture's pinned lease and requires the idle timer to be scheduled, directly observing that request references were released.

The candidate extracts the unchanged request predicate into a static local `InvalidRequest`. Source reconstruction verifies validation still precedes cancellation and that async lease/subscription scopes, freshness, identity/quality rules, sorting, owner lookup and public signatures/MCP attributes remain unchanged. Focused metrics put the entry-point state machine at **26** and validator at **22**, both with full line/branch coverage. All reported implementations have full executable-line coverage and at least 91.67% branch coverage. One nullable-network branch in the row selector remains unhit; rows are selected from that network before the selector runs.

Performance comparison validates the output session GUID against its own client, requires exactly two protocol occurrences, then normalizes only that random GUID for response fingerprint comparison. All other fields are compared. Repeated-query timing uses real disposable system timers with logical clock readings, avoiding the manual helper's retained timer history. Benchmark inputs/publications, physical capture, actual service timing and installed-service interoperability are distinct scopes.

### Existing behavior issue: final-newline hash acceptance

Both compiled copies accept a signed asset whose hash consists of 64 hexadecimal characters followed by LF, returning the original 65-character value. The regex's `$` boundary permits this final-newline case. This is confirmed independently for portable and installer assets by `SignedHashesWithFinalLineFeedRetainTheirExistingAcceptance`. Inference from the unchanged `VerifyFileAsync` source: its exact ordinal-insensitive digest comparison subsequently rejects this value, causing late verification failure rather than early manifest rejection. No trust bypass is established. This inconsistency is recorded for a separate behavior-changing fix; this batch neither trims nor rejects it. Malformed signed JSON/version exception variants are also preserved rather than normalized.

## Remaining work and risks

The complete sorted inventory is [artifacts/crap/remaining.csv](../artifacts/crap/remaining.csv), with module, class, method, signature, source, complexity, line/branch coverage, score and next work for every entry above 30. The raw baseline/final reports and machine-readable metrics remain under `artifacts/crap/`. These are local, ignored verification artifacts; this dated Markdown report is the durable record.

All 308 remaining entries are **not remediated**, rather than suppressed or declared safe. None of those entries are in MonCore. Important next candidates include:

| Method | CRAP | Why it remains / next action |
|---|---:|---|
| `NetworkSetupBroker.IsFailurePhase` (GUI and CLI) | 58 each | Full line coverage and 87.9% branch coverage; generated string dispatch has complexity 58. Retain the clear literal predicate; a metric-only rewrite is unwarranted |
| `WindowsHistoryEventReader.ReadLog` | 82.5 | Controlled iterator boundary was rejected after detected latency regressions; original source restored, 82.5 retained. See the rejected enumeration attempt; message formatting is remediated |
| `SetupService.Install` callback | 600 | Existing protected-folder fixtures require an administrator token; establish a minimal controlled boundary or validate in a disposable elevated environment |
| `UpdateRuntime.SignalReady` | 42 | Requires controlled healthy signaling, session-start and transaction boundaries; preserve actual transactions and native events |

The response-budget batch reproduces an existing internal-envelope fixed-point hazard in bounded owned children, as recorded above. Reachability through current bounded production callers remains unestablished. A separate behavior-changing policy decision is needed before adding an exit/failure guard; this remediation deliberately preserves the existing behavior.

Large UI methods such as `MainWindow.ApplyTheme` (31,862) and diagnostic smoke orchestration remain in the inventory. The test-only baseline does not execute many of those interactive paths. Running smoke modes changes the measured scope; it must not be presented as an improvement from this refactor or a substitute for behavior assertions.

These are follow-up requirements, not findings that each method is impossible to refactor safely. The completed batches establish behavioral evidence for the changed persistence validators, session accounting/frame logic, ranking orchestration, resource-trend ingestion, restart parsing/writing, service-tree capture, connection totals and capture-rule engine, session network-owner attribution, incident timeline calculations, connection query grouping/summaries, connection CSV formatting, incident event placement, controlled service-action orchestration, catalog enumeration, ETW callback direction/queue accounting and ownership/lifetime resolution. They do not satisfy the original repository-wide objective. Prioritize methods scoring above 50, ordered by production risk: protected setup and other production-critical native/process-control methods first, with SignalReady 42 deferred, then the remaining native, CLI/MCP and UI hotspots while establishing controlled native service/ownership fixtures before lower-risk UI/diagnostic numerical hotspots.

Store verification passed for the restart-reader, restart-writer, Windows service-control, service-catalog, ETW callback, ownership, queue/lifecycle, clock/event/reconciliation, service power-transition, ledger snapshot, installation/ACL policy, pipe snapshot preparation, setup native-protection, archive entry copying, read-only native query, protected-tree/inventory, pipe identity/PID, service snapshot validation, MCP hardware projection, performance aggregate, sampling lifecycle, installer-registration, archive-history, recorded-performance-history, response-budget, MCP process-traffic, service-query, connection-query, process-list, signed-manifest and tool-installation/lifecycle batches; other portable batches did not run it separately.
